stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics annual averages: unemployment rates and Consumer Price Index changes, 1970-1980. Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.14; 5 Steps Ch. 28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text:
Inflation and unemployment, annual averages (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics):

| Year | Inflation (change in consumer prices) | Unemployment rate |
| 1970 | 5.7% | 4.9% |
| 1974 | 11.0% | 5.6% |
| 1975 | 9.1% | 8.5% |
| 1979 | 11.3% | 5.8% |
| 1980 | 13.5% | 7.1% |

stem: Which year in the table shows both inflation above 8 percent and unemployment above 8 percent?

options.misconception: In 1970 inflation was 5.7 percent and unemployment was 4.9 percent, so neither was above 8 percent.
In 1979 inflation was 11.3 percent, but unemployment was only 5.8 percent.
In 1980 inflation was 13.5 percent, but unemployment was 7.1 percent, below 8 percent.

rationales.A: In 1970 both numbers were under 6 percent, so 1970 cannot be the year both topped 8 percent.
rationales.B: In 1975 inflation was 9.1 percent and unemployment was 8.5 percent, the only row where both are above 8 percent.
rationales.C: In 1979 inflation topped 11 percent, but unemployment was only 5.8 percent, so the row fails the second half.
rationales.D: In 1980 inflation was the highest in the table, but unemployment was 7.1 percent, below 8 percent.
rationales.general:
1. Read across each row and check both columns, not just one.
2. In 1970 both numbers are low, and in 1974, 1979, and 1980 one of the two is below 8 percent.
3. Only 1975 has both numbers above 8 percent: inflation 9.1 percent and unemployment 8.5 percent.
Remember: When a question asks for two conditions at once, check both columns in every row.
